41.13: Even when he performed the penance thus, nothing happened. After a great deal of time he became miserable and his sorrow turned into anger.
41.14: When he was overwhelmed with anger, drops of tears fell from his eyes. From those drops of tears goblins and ghosts originated.
41.15: Thereupon, the infuriated lord Brahma, abandoned his life. Thereafter, Rudra in the form of Prana ( vital breath) appeared through the mouth of lord Brahma.
41.16: The lord, having a lustre resembling that of the rising sun became Ardhanarisvara ( male-cum-female form).. He divided himself into eleven' parts and settled down there.
41.17: With half a portion of himself Ardhanarisvara, the soul of all, created Uma. She created Laksmi, Durga and Saras- vati.
41.18: (She further created) Varna, Raudri, Mahamaya, Vaisnavi the lotus-eyed goddess, Kalavikarim, Kali residing in the lotu.s, goddess Balavikarini, Balapramathinf, Sarvabhuatada- man!, (the suppressor of all living beings) and Manonmani. Similarly thousands of other women were created by her. Accom- panied by those ladies and the Rudras, Mahadeva,ParameSvara the lord of the three worlds stood in front of lord Brahma Paramesthin who was the soul of all but was now lying dead.
41.19: Lord MaheSvara, the sympathetic son of Brahma, granted him vital airs.
41.20: Then Rudra the lord of Devas was delighted and he spoke these pleasant words to Brahma who regained his life a little.
41.21: O highly blessed lord Brahma, O preceptor of the worlds do not be afraid; the vital airs have been established here in your heart. Hence, O lord get up.

45.3: Formerly, I had mentioned to you about the shape and features of the Cosmic Egg. I shall now describe the features of the worlds in the cosmic Egg. The Earth, the firmament, Svah, Mahab, Jana, Tapas and Satya — these seven are the splendid worlds originating from the Cosmic Egg.

45.5: It is occupied by Ananta, Mucukunda and king Bali who is the resident of Patala and Svarga. O brahmins, Rasatala is rocky, Talatala is full of gravels, Sutala is yellow and Vitala has the lustre of coral.
45.6: Atala is white. Tala is black. O men of good holy rites, the extent of all the Talas below is as much as that of the earth, viz., 1000 yojanas each. 47.1: King Priyavrata crowned his eldest son Agnidhra who was the eldest inheritor and who was a loveable son of great strength, as the king of Jambild\npa.*'
47.3: O leading brahmins, he was an ascetic and a great devotee of Siva. He was a young man engaged in the worship of Siva. He was prosperous and intelligent and he possessed many cows.
47.4: He had nine sons at par with Prajapatis. All of them were followers of Mahevara and devoted to Mahadeva.
47.5: His eldest son was known as Nabhi. Kimpurusa was his (Nabhi's) younger brother. The third son was Harivar?a. The fourth son was Ilavrta.
47.6: Ramya was the fifth; the sixth was Hiramnan. Kuru was the seventh. Bhadrava was the eighth.
47.7: The ninth was Ketumala. Understand their lands now. The subcontinent of Nabhi inherited from his father is called Hema which lies in the south.
47.8: He gave Kimpurusa the subcontinent Hemakuta. He gave the subcontinent called Naisadha to Hari.
47.9: To Ilavrta he gave the midlands encircling the moun- tain Meru. He gave Ramya the subcontinent around Nllacala.
47.10: The subcontinent Sveta to the north of it was given to Hiranman. He gave Kuru the subcontinent Smga Var?a which is to the north of it.
47.11: He gave the subcontinent round about Malyavan to Bhadrava. He gave Gandhamadana to Ketumala.
47.12: These are the nine great subcontinents in brief. After crowning his sons as the kings in those subcontinents, Agmdhra*®® the virtuous became engaged in penance. After purifying himself by penance he became engaged in the study of the Vedas.
47.13: After being engaged in the study of the Vedas he became engaged in meditation on Siva. There is natural per- fection in all the eight excellent subcontinents beginning with Kimpurusa. Without any strain the subjects are always happy. The opposite of joy is not seen in them. They have no fear from death or old age. They have neither Dharma nor Adharma. There is no distinction such as the excellent, the middling and the base. In all these eight subcontinents there are no subdivi- sions of yugas.
47.14: According to Agnldhra was the eldest ion of Priyavrata. But according to a Viyu venion he was the son of Priyavrata*! daughter.
47.15: Those who die in a holy centre of Rudra whether mobile or immobile whether devotees or casual visitors are reborn there.
47.16: For their benefit eight holy centres were created by Rudra. In all those places Mahadeva was always present.
47.17: By seeing Mahadeva in their hearts the residents of the eight holy centres were always happy. He alone was the greatest goal unto them all.
47.18: I shall now recount tiic country of Nabhi marked by *hima' (snow; i.c. Bharatavarsa as mentioned below). The intelligent Nabhi begot a son of Merude\d, Rabha by name who was a great king adored by all ksatriyas. A heroic son Bharata was born to Rsabha. He was the eldest among his hundred sons.
47.19: $abha who was fond of his son Bharata crowned him as king. By adopting the path of knowledge and detach- ment he conquered the serpents of his sense-organs; by all means he stabilised Is vara, the supreme Atman, within his own heart; he was immersed in devout feelings; he observed fasts; he wore bark garments and matted hair. He retired into dark- ness (i.e. solitary place). Devoid of all desires and his doubts all cleared, (in the end) he attained the great region of Siva. He gave the subcontinent to the south of the mountain Himavat to Bharata. Hence learned men call that subcontinent as Bharata Vara*®® after his name. Bharata's son was the virtuous Sumati. Bharata entrusted the kingdom to his care. After transferring the royal glory to his son the king entered the forest for penance.

48.1: In the middle of this Jambu Dvipa is the great moun- tain Meru*®®- It is the most excellent among the mountains, having many peaks full of jewels.
48.2: It is reputed to be eightyfour thousand yojanas in height. It has entered sixteen thousand yojanas beneath the ground and it extends to sixteen thousand yojanas.
48.3: Since it is stationed like a shallow plate the extent on the top is thirty-two thousand yojanas. Three times its width is its girth at the ridges.
48.4: It is rendered golden due to the auspicious contact with the body of Mahesa. It resembles the flower of the Dhattura plant (thorn apple). It is the abode of all Devas.
48.5: It is the sporting ground for Devas. It is full of miracles. The toCal width and extent of this mountain is a hundred thousand yojanas.
48.6: O leading brahmins, beneath the earth its extent is sixteen thousand yojanas. The remaining part of that moun- tain is above the earth. The extent at the root is thus sixteen thousand yojanas and the extent above, they say, is twice the extent at the root.
48.7: In the cast it has the lustre of the ruby; in the south it resembles gold; in the west it shines like the blue stone and in the north it has the coral lustre.
48.8: In the eastern side of this mountain is Amaravati (the city of Indra). It is full of mansions of different kinds. It is thronged by different groups of Devas. It is surrounded by clusters of jewels.
48.9: It has many ornamental gateways of different shapes bedecked in gold and jewels. The arches at the gateways are rendered wonderful with gol'd, with jewels set in. Thousands of women throng the roadways. They aie clever in conversation and elocution. They are bedecked in all ornaments. They stoop down due to the weight of their heavy breasts and their eyes
48.11: In the south-eastern side of the mountain is Tejasv- ini the city of the fire god. It is divine and similar to Amara- vati. It is endowed with all means of pleasures.
48.12: O sages, most excellent among those who have self- control, in the southern side of the mountain is the city of Yama Vaivasvata. It is full of many divine abodes built in gold and very splendid.
48.13: In the south-west is the splendid dark-colourcd city Suddhavati.2® Similarly in the north-west is the splendid cuy Gandhavati. The city in the north is Mahodaya and that in the north-east is Yasovati. Thus cities in all the quarters always shine.
48.14: There are the abodes of Brahma, Visnu and Maheia as well as of others on it. Thus the mountain endowed with all means of pleasures and containing many lakes, is the most excellent among the mountains.
48.15: It is full of Siddhas, Yaksas, Gandharvas, sages and the four kinds of living beings.
48.16: O leading brahmins, on the mountain towaids the left, stands a palace of seven storeys that is as clear as pure crystal. It is as extensive as though it has a thousand landing grounds. There stays lord Siva of great arms, whose eyes are the sun, moon and fire. He is seated in a gemset throne along with the goddess and the six-faced deity Karltikeya.
48.17: The palace of Visnu is also there. It extends to half of that of lord Siva and he (Visnu) stays there. In the south is the divine palace of the lotus-born deity Brahma. It is full of rubies. There is the city of Indra which is very large. There is the beautiful city of Yama. There are the cities of

48.19: Some part of it, is the ground for the practice of yoga. In some places are the grounds for enjoyment of plea- sures. There is a splendid palace with seven storeys resem- bling the rising sun.
48.20: It is the splendid palace of Nandi and the chieftain of the Ganas is seated there in the midst of six-faced deity, Ganea, thousands of Ganas, Suyasa of beautiful eyes, the mothers and Madana. The river Jambu**® flows round the base of this mountain.

49.1: The first Dvipa, it is said, extends to a thousand yojanas. The other Dvipas successively extend to twice the previous one.
49.2: The earth along with all the oceans is stated as ex- tending to fifty crores of yojanas. It consists of seven Dvipas. It is splendid and is surrounded by the Lokaloka mountain.®® The mountain Nila is to the north of the Meru. The Sveta is to the north of this and the Srngi is still further north of Sveta. O brahmins, these three are the mountains of the sub-con- tinents in the north.
49.3: The Jathara® and the Devakuta® are the mountains in the eastern quarter. The Nisadha*®® is to the south of the Meru. Still south of it is the mountain Hemakuta.®' The Himavat is to its south.
49.4: To the west of the Meru there are two mountains: Mal- yavan®*® and Gandhamadana.®® These two extend towards the north.
49.5: On the eastern side of Meru there are two mountains, namely the Jatha &nd the Devakuta which run north to south and stretch up to the Nila (Tien Shan) and Nifadha mountains (Fayu 35.8). Jathara is identified with Kuruk-Tagh and Devakuta with Altin Tagh — Nan Shan Tsing-ling of Sinkiang and Northern China. The Geography qf the Pufdoas* PP» 99-100.
49.6: Niadha: Sp. places it to Che south of the Meru, along with the Himavat and Hemakilta. It represents Hindukush Kunlun chain.
49.7: Hemakfita: a sacred hill situated to the north of M&nasacovara It represents Ladakh-Kailash-Trans-Himalayan chain.
49.8: All these leading mountains are frequented by the Siddhas and Caranas. The inter>space between two mountains is nine thousand yojanas in each case.
49.9: This sub-continent south of the Himavat is known as Bharata. Hemakuta is beyond that, llie sub-continent within it is Kimpuru§a. Ni$adha is beyond HemakQti. Its sub-conti- nent is called Harivar§a. Beyond Harivar§a and Meru is the splendid Ilavrta. Beyond Ilavrta is Nila and the sub-continent Ramyaka. Beyond Ramyaka is Sveta and the sub-continent known as Hiraaya. The mountain beyond Hiramaya is known as Srhgi and sub-continent beyond it is JCuru. The two Var§as one in the south and one in the north (i.e. Himavarsa and Ramyaka) are stationed like an arch.
49.10: The other four are horizontal in shape. Ilavrta is in the middle; to the west and east of the Meru there are two sub- continents and they are smaller ( than the four mentioned before).
49.11: The area above Nisadha is known as the northern Vedyardha (half of the whole Dvipa which is conceived as a sacrificial altar). Thus there are three Var§as in the southern half and three Varsas in the northern half.
49.12: Ilavirta with the Meru in the middle is in the midst of the two halves.
49.13: Its length and width is similar to that of Malyavan. These six Var§a mountains of good ridges extend to the east and are bounded on both sides by the Eastern and Western seas.
49.14: Himavat is full of snow. The Hemakilta contains gold. The Nisadha is also golden resembling the morning sun.
49.15: The golden Meru which extends upwards has four colours. Its girth is symmetrical and cylindrical. It rises high.
49.16: The mountain Nila is full of Lapis Lazuli stones. The «§veta is white in colour and full of gold. The three-peaked mountain Srngi has the colour of the feathers of the peacock and contains gold.
49.17: Four lofty trees grow on these as though they are the flagstaffs of the Dvipas. The great tree on the peak of the moun- tain Mandara is the Kadamba, the king of flagstaffs. It has long hanging branches. It acts as a caityapadapa (holy big tree in a sacred temple).
49.18: There are groves in the four directions. Understand them by their names. The forest grove in the east is Caitraratha; in the south it is Gandhamadana; it is Vaibhraja in the west; in the north it is the garden of Savitr (sun).
49.19: The sages sport about there on the mountains and in the gardens.
49.20: To the west of the lake Sitoda there stand Surapa, Mahabala, Kumuda, Madhuman, Aiijana, Mukuta. Krsa, Pandura, Sahasraikhara, the leading hills Parijata andSrirhga. These are the prominent excellent mountains frequented by Devas in the western quarter and they contain shrines of Rudra.
49.21: The extremely powerful mountains to the north of the lake Mahabhadra are being stated now succinctly.
49.22: They are: — Sahkhakuta, Mahaaila, Vrabha, Haihsaparvata, Naga, Kapila, Indrasaila, Sanuman, Nila, Kantakafhga, Sataihga, Pufpakoa, Praaila, Virajas, Varahaparvata, Mayura and Jarudhi.® All these are stationed in the north.
49.23: There are thousands of divine palaces of the trident- bearing lord on those divine hills.
49.24: In the interstices of these leading hills there arc many internal water reservoirs, lakes and parks.
49.25: Thanks to the favour of Paramesthin, Devas, sages, Siddhas purified by their devotional thoughts of Siva reside here along with their families in their respective abodes.
49.26: The different deities reside in the various forests as follows: —
49.27: J&nidhi: This range is identified with the Kirghiz-ZaUai Al-Tau, Ketmen chain. GF. p. 82.
49.28: The glorious Garuda stays in Vaikuntha. The prosperous Nilalohita stays in Karaftja.®®® The Vasus live in Vasudhara.
49.29: Sitanta: It means *end of cold', i.e. ''a range which marks the dividing line between the cold and hot regions. If the river Kizil-Su repre- sents the head waters of the Puraic river Sita, Sitanta is obviously the Kashghar range, i.e. the last longitudinal range of the Pamir region facing the Tarim basin, on the east. It is a range which, to a traveller coming from the east across the hot and sandy Tarim Basin, stands athwart the route to- wards the west and promises a cool climate beyond. It is an effective climatic barrier which separates a hot and dry desert on the east from the cold pla- teau on the west. Coming from the west it literally marks the *end of cold* and is thereCore rightly qualified for its name, Sitanta". GP. pp. 100-101.
49.30: Kumuda: Peak Barzengi (16,456 feet) beyond the Pakshif Pass.
49.31: Most of the mountains mentioned in this chapter are not Identifiable.
49.32: There are seven holy spots on the mountain Ratnadhara belonging to the noble seven sages. They contain the abodes of the Siddhas as well.
49.33: The great abode of Prajapati is on the mountain ekarhga. Durga and others stay on the Gajaiiaila and the Vasus on the Sumedha.
49.34: The Adityas, Rudras and Asvins have their abodes in eighty divine cities on the mountain Hemakaka.
49.35: There are five hundred crores of abodes of the Rakiasas on the Sunila mountain which has five peaks with five crores of cities in each.
49.36: The hundred cities of the Yakas of unmeasured pro- wess are on the Satarnga; the cities of Kadraveyas are on the mountain Tamrabha; the city of Guha is on the Viha hill.
49.37: O excellent sages, the abode of Suparna is on the Svetodara; the abode of Kubera is on the Pisacaka and that of Vi§nu is on the Harikuta.
49.38: The residence of lord Siva*®* along with Uma is in the cave of mountain Srikaiatha. Srikatha is the overlord of all the chiefs of Devas* Undoubtedly the Cosmic Egg functions by the grace of Srikaitla. Ananta, 1'a and others are severally the protectors of the Cosmic Egg. They are called Vidycvaras as well as Cakravartins (Emperors).

50.1: The glorious Garuda stays in Vaikuntha. The prosperous Nilalohita stays in Karanja.®® The Vasus live in Vasudhara.
50.2: Sitanta: It means 'end of cold', i.e. "a range which marks the dividing line between the cold and hot regions. If the river Kizil-Su repre- sents the head waters of the Puranic river Sita, Sitanta is obviously the Kashghar range, i.e. the last longitudinal range of the Pamir region facing the Tarim basin, on the east. It is a range which, to a traveller coming from the east across the hot and sandy Tarim Basin, stands athwart the route to- wards the west and promises a cool climate beyond. It is an effective climatic barrier which separates a hot and dry desert on the east from the cold pla- teau on the west. Coming from the west it literally marks the 'end of cold* and is therefore rightly qualified for its name, Sitanta". GP. pp. loo-ioi.

50.4: Most of the mountains mentioned in this chapter are not iden tillable.
50.5: There are seven holy spots on the mountain Ratnadhara, belonging to the noble seven sages. They contain the abodes of the Siddhas as well.
50.6: The great abode of Prajapati is on the mountain ekaSrhga. Durga and others stay on the Gajaaila and the Vasus on the Sumedha.
50.7: The Adityas, Rudras and Asvins have their abodes in eighty divine cities on the mountain Hemakaksa.
50.8: There are five hundred crorcs of abodes of the Raksasas on the Sunlla mountain which has five peaks with five croies of cities in each.
50.9: The hundred cities of the Yaksas of unmeasured pio- wess are on the Satasrnga; the cities of Kadraveyas are on the mountain Tamrabha; the city of Guha is on the Visakha hill.
50.10: O excellent sages, the abode of Suparna is on the Svetodara; the abode of Kubera is on the Pisacaka and that of Visnu is on the Harikuta.

51.1: The beautiful forest Bhutavana, the residence of the different groups of Bhutas (goblins), is on the highly splendid mountain Devakuta. This mountain has great peaks. It is splendid and devoid of impurities. It is made up by gold, Lapis Lazuli, rubies, emeralds, lustrous Gomeda (onyx) and other precious stones. It ranges in a number of branches on all sides. It is adorned with all kinds of trees such as Campaka, Aoka, Punnaga, Bakula, Asana and Parijata. It contains many flocks of birds and herds of elephants. It is variegated in colour with hundreds of minerals. It abounds in wonderful specimens of flowers. Its ridges are covered with bunches of flowers hanging down. Various kinds of animals live therein. It contains many springs and fountains with pure and sweet water. It is adorned with many waterfalls and cascades strewn with flowers. It is beautified by running streams with rafts of flowers floating on them. This Bhutavana®®' has pleasing colours. It contains many trees with great roots and stems. The thick shade of these trees spreads to ten yojanas all-round.

51.3: Bhutavana: BhUta is a name of Siva; BhUta-vana— Siva's forest.
51.4: In that mansion of Siva there are many apart- ments decorated with garlands of never-fading flowers of dif- ferent colours. There are many raised platforms (Mantjapas) of different shapes and sizes with crystal columns. The leading goblins (Bhutas) adored by Brahma, Indra and Upendra stay there. There are many Pramathas with their faces resembling those of boars, elephants, lions, bears, tigers, camels, vultures, owls, deer, humped bulls and goats. They are stout and huge like great mountain peaks. They are terrible with having huge arms. Some have green hairs on their heads. They are of dif- ferent shapes and sizes. They are seated in all possible pos- tures and positions. There arc splendid Ganas such as Nan- diivara, with bright beaming faces and spotless character. They possess supernatural qualities and they resemble Brahma, Indra and Visnu. The place is never devoid of crowds of im- mortal beings, (i.e. Devas) who worship the lord of Bhutas (i.e. Siva) there, always.
51.5: Sankara, Mahadeva, the lord of Pramhathas is worshipped by the Siddhas, Devas, Gandharvas, Brahma, and others such as Upendra. They use these musical instruments (drums, etc.) in the course of their worship— Jharj haras (cym- bals) conches, Patahas, Bhcris, Diidimas, Gomukhasw During their worship they sing in low, middle and high pitches; they also jump, dance and shout in joy. Sankara when being worshipped thus appears as though he has divided into two the beautiful peak (Kailasa) having the lustre of the conch.
51.6: Kailasa®® is the abode of Kubera, the king of Yaksas as well as other noble beings.
51.7: There too, Siva the lord of Devas has a great abode. He stays there always accompanied by Uma and the chiefs of Ganas.

51.10: On its northern bank is the splendid abode of Lord Siva, finished with lapis lazuli and other gems. He, the unchang- ing lord, stays there.
51.11: O brahmins, on the eastern and southern banks of the river Kanakananda there is a forest with thousands of Brah- mins,animals and birds.
51.12: There- also the lord sports in a mansion similar to the one on the mountain (Kailasa ) along with Uma and chief Ganas. On the western bank of the Nanda®, a little towards the South there is the city Rudrapuri. It is full of many man- sions. In these also Lord Siva assuming hundreds of forms sports about along with Uma and the Ganas It is called Sivalaya (abode of Siva). Thus there are hundreds and thousands of shrines of Siva in every Dvipa, O excellent sages, on the moun- tains, in the forests, on the banks of rivers, lakes and on the junctions of waters.

52.1: O best of Brahmins, on every sub-continent there are many holy rivers always full of water and originating from great lakes. They flow in all four directions: east, south, north and west.
52.2: The storehouse of water in the sky which is called Soma (moon) is the support of all living beings. To Devas, it is the receptacle of nectar.
52.3: From this has originated the river of auspicious waters and it flows in the firmament. With nectarine waters it functions through the seventh path of the wind. This river follows the path of the luminaries. It is frequented by groups of luminaries, and by thousands and crores of stars of the sky.®® Just like the moon it also goes round and round every day.
52.4: After going beyond all the mountains partially it enters the great sea at the behest of lord Siva.
52.5: The Kurus in Kuruvar?a are those who have fallen down there from the heavenly world. All of them are bom by copulation. They are fond of milk®® and live on milk diet.
52.6: They love one another and have qualities simillar to those of the Cakravaka birds. They are devoid of ailments and sorrow and perpetually seek happiness.
52.7: They live up to fourteen thousand five hundred years. They have great virility, but do not associate with other women.
52.10: K|lri9a|}t*--<>fiiiflk-white complexion. Contrast with KAl&h V. 12.
52.11: All the residents of the Kunivarsa like the heaven- dwellers die simultaneously. They are delighted and flouri* shing. They take in all kinds of cooked rice and nectar.
52.12: They shine always like the moon; they have perpetual youth; they are dark in colour in their bodies and always wear ornaments.
52.13: Among all the sub-continents in the Jambudvipa the sub-continent of Kuruvarsa is extremely splendid. There is a magnificent palace of the moon-crested lord liva. It has the lustre of the moon.
52.14: In the sub-continent Bharatavarsa* men are auspi- cious and their longevity depends on their Karmans. They are said to live for a hundred years. They are of different colours and their bodies are small.
52.15: They are engaged in the worship of different Devas; they experience the fruits of different kinds of Karmans; they are richly endowed with knowledge and with different mate- rials. They are weak and have ver.' little pleasures.
52.16: Some of them have gone to Indradvipa®* and some to Kaseruka. Others have gone to Tamradvipa and some to the country Gabhastimat. Some have gone to Naga- dvlpa, some to Saumyadvipa, and others to the Dvipa of Gandharvas as well as of Varuna. Some of them are Mlecchas and Pulindas born of different castes.
52.17: In the Eastern parts of the Dvipa are the Kiratas; in the western extremities the Yavanas; in the middle the Brahmins Ksatriyas and Vaiiyas. The Sudras are everywhere.®®
52.18: The glorification of Bhrata is one of the common topics in the PurSas.
52.19: Bh&rata is one of the nine khanas of Jambudvipa; the other eight being Indradvlpa, Kaserumim, Tamra-varna, Gabhastiman, Naga, Saumya, Gandharva, and Varuna.
52.20: The Puranas are conscious of the foreign tribes that surrounded Bharata (cf. Mata, 50. 75-76; Mark, 57,8.). The Kiratas mentioned along the eastern limits are probably the uncivilized tribes of the forests and mountains with the Burmese type of features. The Yavanas in the virest are Greeks originally and afterwards the Mohammedans.
52.21: They are established there maintaining themselves by worship, warfare and business dealings (respectively). Mutual dealings in connection with the activities of the dif- ferent castes are related only to virtue, wealth and love. They are interested in their own duties. The conception and pride in performing the duties of the various stages of life are maintained properly.
52.22: It is only here that human beings endeavour for hea- venly pleasures and salvation. O leading sages, only here they pursue the duties specified for each yuga,®*® not elsewhere.
52.23: In the sub-continent Kimpurusa men live up to ten thousand years. Men are golden-complexioned and women resemble the celestial damsels.
52.24: They are devoid of ailments and sorrow. They are all purified by meditations on Siva. They have Sattva qualities and the lustre of gold. They live on Plaksa fruits along with their wives,
52.25: The people there have the lustre of lotuses. Their faces resemble the lotus. Their eyes are like the petals of the lotus. They have the fragrance of the petals of the lotus. They are purified by their meditation on Siva.
52.26: The juice of the Jambu fruits constitutes their diet. They are sweet-scented. They have no duties to perform.®® They have come there from the world of Devas and have neither death nor old age.
52.27: Since Bharata alone it Karma-Bhumi (land for performing action) » the yuga-dharmas (duties pertaining to yugas) prevail only here. Of. Vifiju cited in ST,
52.28: In the divine sub-continent Ilavrta, the excellent men live their full span of life which is thirteen thousand years.
52.29: By drinking the juice of the Jambu fruits they are not afflicted by old age. They have neither hunger nor fatigue. They do not die a premature death.
52.30: The gold found there is called Jambunada. It is the divine metal. It shines and resembles a glow-worm,
52.31: Thus the persons occupying the nine sub-continents have been recounted by me. Their colour, span of life, diet and other things have been succinctly mentioned and not in detail.

They number thirty three thousands and they live happily on the mountain Nila, full of lapis lazuli, the Siddhas and Brahmarsis devoid of impurities.

They number thirty three thousands and they live happily on the mountain Nila, full of lapis lazuli, the Siddhas and Brahmarsis devoid of impurities.

53.1: There are seven important mountains in each of the seven Dvipas beginning with Plaksa. They extend straight in all directions and form the boundaries of the great continents,
53.2: I shall mention the seven great mountains in the Plaksadvipa. The first mountain is Gomedaka; the second is Candra; the third is Narada; the fourth is Dundubhi; the fifth is Somaka; the sixth Sumanas, the same is called Vaibhava; the seventh is Vaibhraja. These are the seven important moun-- tains in the Plaksa Dvipa.
53.3: There are only seven important mountains in the Salmalidvipa. I shall mention them in order. They arc Kumuda, Uttama, Balahaka Drona, Kanka, Mahisa and Kakudman.
53.4: The bull-emblemed lord of the universe Siva, the deity without impurities, stays there in person in an excellent golden palace accompanied by Uma and Nandin.
53.5: There are two meritorious and splendid Janapadas on either side of the Manasa mountain, and shining like silver. The sub-continent Mahavita*® is on the exterior of the Manasa. The Janapada in the interior is called Dhatakikhanda.*
53.6: The Puskara Dvipa is surrounded by the ocean of sweet water. All round this ocean extends to as much area as the Puskara Dvipa. In girth and extent it is equal to Puskara.
53.7: The seventh ocean is beyond all Dvipas. Thus the comparative sizes of dvipas and oceans are stated.
53.8: The great ocean of sweet waters is stationed envelop- ing the Puskara.
53.9: Beyond that is the situation of the world. The earth is golden and twice in extent. The entire thing is comparable to a single rock.
53.10: Beyond it is the globular mountain of delimitation.
53.11: Mah&vlta and Dbatakikha]?. These are the two provinces of Pufksura-dvipa (identified with Japan, Manchuria and SB Siberia). The mountain M&nasa runs in a circle like a full moon and divides the two provinces. The exterior province is Mahavita and the interior is Dhktakl.
53.12: O brahmins, this earth abides, as long as this visible- cum-invisible mountain exists. Its height is stated to be ten thousand yojanas.
53.13: The extent of the great mountain Lokaloka is also that much. The rays of the sun pass over its inner and nether half,
53.14: In its other half there is perpetual darkness. Hence it is called Lokaloka. Thus, the world Bhur is explained succin- ctly.
53.15: The Bhuvarloka is upto the sun. O excellent sages, the Svarloka is upto Dhruva (pole star). There are seven wheels of the wind, viz., Avaha, Pravaha, Anuvaha, Sam- vaha, Vivaha, Paravaha and Parivaha, O brahmins, these arc the seven wheels of the wind.
53.16: The solar sphere is one hundred thousand yojanas above the surface of the earth. Above it the chariot of the sun is sixteen thousand yojanas. The Meru is eighty-four thousand yojanas above the surface of the earth. The Maharloka extends to a crore of yojanas above Dhruva. O brahmins, the Janaloka extends to two crores of yojanas beyond Maharloka. Tapo- loka extends to four crores of yojanas beyond Jamaloka. Beyond that the Brahmaloka extends to six crores of yojanas. O brahmins, the holy worlds in this Cosmic Egg are thus seven.
53.17: Beneath the seven nether worlds are the crores of hells. They are twentyeight in number beginning with Ghora and ending with Maya.
53.18: All the Pur&as mentioa seven divisions of the strato -sphere.
53.19: Since Pradhana is present everywhere within each of these Cosmic Eggs there are fourteen worlds in all sides as well as above and below. O leading brahmins, the cause of their creation is lord Siva himself. The eight-bodied Siva is present in all the Eggs, in the exterior of the Eggs, in the coverings of the Eggs, in the extremities of the darkness and beyond dark- ness. Wonderful it is, every thing in the universe is the body of the unembodied great Atman, of Mahesa, of the intelligent Mahadeva.
53.20: The lord Siva is infinite. He is devoid of beginning and end. He is the Purusa. He is identical with the seven principles*' beginning from Pradhana. His body is Pradhana itself, having sixteen limbs.*** (i.e. the organs of knowledge, organs of action, elements and mind). He himself is Mahevara and Astatanu (eight-bodied ).
53.21: It is due to the power of His command that the earth is held steady. So also the mountains, clouds, oceans, luminaries, Devas beginning with Indra, those who go about in the aerial chariots as well as the mobile and immobile beings.
53.22: Devas including Indra saw the lord devoid of specific characteristics in the guise of a Yaksa.**®On seeing him they wondered "What is this?" They went to the Yaksa. Unable to come to any conclusion, fire and others exerted themselves but became weak and inefficient.
53.23: O brahmins, in front of that Yaksa the fire-god could not burn even a blade of grass; the wind-God could not shake a blade of grass; all the leading immortal beings failed to exer- cise their respective powers over him.
53.24: At that time, the enemy of Vrtra (i.e. Indra), the lord
53.25: The astamilrti (eight-formed, p. 166) Siva is the house- holder whose mistress is Prakrti, whose subjects are intellect, ego and five subtle elements. His eight-formed body has sixteen parts, viz., five gross elements, five organs of action, five organs of knowledge and the mind.
53.26: At that time the Yaksa vanished. Then the splendid- faced daughter of Himavat, Uma, shining gloriously with many auspicious ornaments appeared in front of him.
53.27: Indra and others asked that unborn daughter of Himavat, Uma, the intensely bright one; — "O Goddess, O excessively refulgent, what is this? O Uma, who was this shining one in the body of Yaksa?"
53.28: On hearing it, Uma said: "the Yaksa is invisible.*' Devas including Indra bowed down to that deity having the gait of a lion, and to Uma unborn and of red, white and black colour.

54.1: In the cast of the Mem, the city of Mahendra is situa- ted on the mountain Manasa; in the south the city of the son of the sun (i.e. Yama); in the west is the city of Varuna and in the north the city of Soma (Moon ). In all these directions, the deities of the quarters are stationed. They are the cities of Amaravatl, Samyamanl, Sukha and Vibha in order.
54.2: Understand the movement of the sun when he has reached quarter over and above the guardians of the quarters in the course of his southern transit.
54.3: In his southern transit the sun rushes on like an arrow that is shot. Taking the multitude of luminaries with him he revolves perpetually.
54.4: O brahmins, when the lordly sun comes to the extremity of the city of Indra the sunrise is seen by all the people in Sam- yamanl.
54.5: At the same time in Sukha vat! the sun is seen as at the close of the night. But in Vibha. the lord, the eye of the universe, i.e. the Sun sets.
54.6: It has been mentioned by me that just as he absorbs waters in Amaravatl so also he, the traverser of the firmament, after reaching Samyamanl, Sukha** and Vibha, absorbs waters.
54.7: When there is afternoon in Agneyl (i.e. south-east), O brahmins, it is forenoon in the south-west. When it is terrible latter half of the night in the north-west, it is the earlier part of the night in the north-east. Similarly, when the sucker of waters (i.e. the sun) moves about in the middle of Puskara®®* the mountain to the north of Manasa, he traverses a thirtieth part of the earth in a Muhurta (48 mts). Understand this number in yojanas travelled in a Muhurta.
54.8: The speed of the noble-souled sun per Muhurta is three million one hundred and fifty thousand yojanas. When the sun moves to the southern quarter with this speed from the north through the middle of Puskara during his northern transit and when he moves into the northern direction (from
54.9: Sukh& or Su9&. It la the capital of Varuna in the western direc- tion and it the tame as Sus& of the ancient Achemenian empire in Iran.
54.10: Pufkara or sky, atmospheric region. Cf. Vilva cited in ST. «<Pu|karam pahkid vyomni**.
54.11: Just as the middle of the potter's wheel moves more slowly (than the end part) so also in the Uttarayana (northern transit) the sun moves slowly.
54.12: Hence he traverses a smaller area in the course of a longer time. That chariot of the sun is occupied by Adityas, sages, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Gramanis, Serpents, and Rak- sasas. The thousand-rayed sun emits his rays in front, behind, below and above. Thereby he illuminates the excellent assembly of Brahma. During the sandhyas (dawn and dusk) the brahmins and sages offer water-libations. With these waters, the sun kills the demons as and when they come near him and then goes ahead.
54.13: A star space is 360 or 13® i3*i Star space is thus equal to 180. In other words the whole consists of 360* which is the space of the 27 constellations Afvini etc. The sun is visible at any time only on half of the sphere (called day). Hence half of the sphere is 180° or star spaces. The reference here is to that day when the day time is shortest (i.e. 9 hours 36 minutes) and night longest (14 hours 24 minutes) which occurs in India in Kashmir.
54.14: Just as the wheel whirls slowly at the nave, so also Dhruva whirls like the lump of clay in the middle.
54.15: Those who know the ancient lore, say that thirty muhurtas constitute a day and a night during which the sun traverses the space in between the two limits (i.e. the solstitial points). Just as the nave of the wheel of the porter remains there alone (i.e. without moving) so also Auttanapada (i.e. Dhruva) rotates (without moving) as the leader of the lumina- ries along with the planets.
54.16: The group of the sages and the luminaries moves in accordance with his will (mind). Presided over by him the sun, along with the wind, takes up water from everywhere.
54.17: For the welfare of creatures, the waters have been evolved by lord Siva as their ultimate resort. The waters alone constitute Bhu, Bhuvah, Svah, anna (cooked rice) as well as nectar. The waters are the vital breaths of the worlds, the living beings, the worlds themselves. Of what avail is much talk? The world of mobile and immobile beings is constituted by the waters.
54.18: O brahmins, the cloud originating from the smoke of the dead bodies brings about evil. The cloud originating from the smoke of the fire during magic rites brings about the destruction of living beings.
54.19: Thus there is weal or woe unto the worlds due to diffe- rent kinds of smokes. Hence a man shall stifle the smoke arising from the black magic rites.
54.20: If a brahmin were to perform black magic rites with- out covering up the smoke thereof, he will wantonly become the cause of destruction of the world.
54.21: O men of holy rites, the clouds that are receptacles of waters shower waters at the behest of the wind for six months for the welfare of the worlds.
54.22: The thunder pertains to the wind; the lightning arises from fire. O leading sages, the origin of snow from those clouds is in three ways.
54.23: The word abhra is derived thus: — na bhrayanti yatah (since they do not become destroyed).
54.24: The showers of the clouds Paundras, (i.e., those falling in the land of Pundra) are accompanied by lightning, arc cool and hence conducive to plant (growth). They are ice-cool and look like the spray of waters from elephants' trunks.
54.25: The clouds called Gangas originate from the waters of Ganga. Through the wind in the Paravaha region these agitate the mountains, rivers and elephants of the quarters.
54.26: The water separated from the clouds goes from one mountain to another. The wind Paravaha takes the cloud to the Himavat mountain.
54.27: O brahmins, the remaining shower after crossing the
54.28: Pufkardyit: Puskara, Avarta, etc. coinprise a class of clouds that rain in torrents at the dissolution of the world.
54.29: The showers have been recounted now. They are of two types being conducive to the increase of two types of vege- tation. I shall mention them briefly according to my knowledge.
54.30: The sun of great splendour, the lord with the eye of the universe is the creator of rains. O excellent brahmins, he is the great Iana, Siva himself.
54.31: He alone is the splendour, power and strength, O brahmins. He is fame himself. He is the eye, ear, mind, Mrtyu, soul, Manyu, the quarters and the interstices, truth, order, discipline, wind, firmament, planets, the guardians of the quarters, Visnu, Brahma, Rudra and Mahevara himself.
54.32: This glorious thousand-rayed deity lord Siva is very auspicious. He has eight hands, a body semi-female and three eyes. He is the overlord of Devas. O brahmins, it is due to his favour alone that rain of various kinds occurs. The sun takes up water by his rays in order to give it back thousandfold. There is neither increase nor decrease of water, if we consider it duly. The wind presided over by Dhruva withdraws the rain. It falls off the planet sun and spreads through the sphere of the stars. At the close of the movement, it re-enters the sun and is presided over by Dhruva.

At the close of the movement, it re-enters the sun and is presided over by Dhruva.

55.1: I shall briefly describe the chariot of the sun, moon and other planets as also how the sun traverses drinking up the waters.
55.2: The solar car. Cf. Matsya, Ch. 125. For the 12 Heptads of the solar system Gf. MP,—A Study pp. 21 1-212. The solar system with the sun as the centrel point is conceived as a chariot which moves upto 180 degrees both north and south of the equator (V. 14; also *23'57).
55.3: The golden chariot of the sun is the abode of all Devas. It has a single wheel with five spokes and three naves,
55.4: Its length and breadth is nine thousand yojanas. Twice that length is the distance between the driver's box and the poleshaft.
55.5: The horses are stationed on the side where the wheel is. They are unattached*®® but appear to be yoked. There are seven horses. They are evolved out of the vedic passages and metres.®*®
55.6: The horses are bound to the side of the wheel. The axle is fitted to the poleshaft. The chariot revolves along with the wheel and the horses, and the poleshaft revolves along with the axle.
55.7: The axle prompted by the poleshaft whirls along with the single wheel. It is the intelligent Dhruva (Pole star) that urges the luminaries by means of the wind and the rays (or by the wind which acts as reins).
55.8: There are two reins in the chariot. They are united to the extremities of the yoke and the axle. The chariot tied by means of the reins to the yoke and the axle revolves by the grace of Dhruva.
55.9: As the chariot whirls and moves along the firmament there shall be circles of bright lustre. The extremities of the yoke and the axle are to the right of the chariot.
55.10: When the horses beyond the wheel®*® are pulled by Dhruva by means of reins, both of them (the yoke and axle) as also the reins follow the poleshaft that whirls.
55.11: The extremity of the yoke and the axle of this chariot which has the steed of wind whirls in all directions like a rope fixed to a nail. In the course of Uttarayana as the chariot moves about in the manqlalas the reins increase in size (i.c.
55.12: asadgaih««intarik9agaih ST. those that move in the void.
55.13: The seven horses of the solar car are the seven metres, via., g&yatri, ufQtk, anuftup, brhatl, paAkti, triftup and jagatl.
55.14: Vicakr&ive — when tho horses, wheel and Arua the driver (are secured by Dhruva).
55.15: The distEince between the two solstices consists of one hundred and eighty degrees. The sun moves about the mandalas externally as the reins are being released by Dhruva. He then encircles the mandalas and moves quickly.
55.16: That chariot is occupied by Devas, Adityas sages, Gandharvas, Apsarases as well as serpents, Raksasas, and Gramanis.
55.17: These reside within the sun for two months in succession and develop and nourish the auspicious sun by means of their splendour.
55.18: The sages eulogise the sun by means of hymns. The Gandharvas and Apsarases worship him by music and dance.
55.19: The Gramanis, Yaksas and Bhutas hold the reins. The serpents bear the sun and Yatudhanas (Raksasas) follow him.
55.20: The Valakhilyas surround the sun from his rise to his setting and accompany him. In this manner these reside in the sun for two months in succession.
55.21: O leading brahmins, the following twelve months constitute the human year: — Madhu (Gaitra), Madhava (VaKakha), Sukra (Jyestha), Suci (Asa<Jha), Nabhas (Sra- vana), Nabhasya (Bhadrapada), Isa (Alvina) Crja (Karttika), Sahas (Margair?a) Sahasya (Pau?a), Tapas (Magha) and Tapasya (Phalguna).
55.22: The (six) Rtus (seasons) are Vasantika (Spring), Graima, (summer) Varika (rainy season) Sarad (autumn), Hima (early Winter) and SHira (late Winter)
55.23: The sages are twelve in number. They eulogise the sun by means of hymns. They are: — Pulastya, Pulaha, Atri, Vasistha, Ahgiras, Bhrgu, Bharadvaja, Gautama, Kayapa, Kratu, Jamadagni and Visvamitra.
55.24: The serpents are twelve in number. They bear the great lord Sun. They are: — Vasuki, Kahkanikara, Taksaka, Naga, Elapatra, lahkhapala, Airavata (Iravan), Dhanafijaya Mahapadma, Karkotaka, Kambala and Avatara.
55.25: The twelve excellent Gandharvas worship the sun that takes in water by means of Songs. They are: — Tumburu, Narada, Haha, Huhu, Visvavasu, Ugrasena, Surugi, Paravasu Citrasena, Orriayu, Dhrtaratra and Suryavarcas.
55.26: The twelve Apsarases worship the sun by their charming Tandava dance. They are: — Krtasthala of splendid face, the divine lady Puhjikasthall of splendid hips, Menaka, Saha- janya, Pramloca of sweet smiles, Anumloca, Ghrtacl, VisvacI, UrvasI also known as Purvacitti, the gentle lady Tilottama and Rambha of lotus-like face.
55.27: The twelve Gramanls hold the reins. They are: — Rathakrt, Rathaujas, Rathacitra, Subahu, Rathasvana, Varuna, Su§ena, Senajit, Tarksya, Ari§tanemi, Ksatajit and Satyajit.
55.28: Then there are twelve Yatudhanas. Wielding their weapons they accompany the sun. They are: — Raksoheti, Praheti, Paurueya, Badha, Sarpa, Vyaghra, Apa, Vata, Vidyut, Divakara, Brahmopeia the leading Raksasa and Yajhopcta.
55.55: These deities occupy the sun for two months (in diffe- rent groups as mentioned above). These twelve Hep tads are the governing forces during the twelve months of the solar year.
55.56: The deities nourish and develop the sun by their splendour. The sages eulogise the sun by the hymns of the Vedas. The Gandharvas and the Apsarases worship him by their music and dance. The Gramanis, Yaksas and Bhutas hold the reins; the serpents bear the sun, and Yatudhanas follow him; Valakhilyas lead the sun to his setting place after surrounding him at the time of his rise.
55.57: The sun is nourished by the splendour of all these. The sun blazes in accordance with their splendour, penance, yogic power, Mantras, Dharmas and strength. These stay in the sun in groups, for two months each.
55.58: The sages, Devas, Gandharvas, Serpents, groups of Apsarases, Gramanis, Yak§as, and Yatudhanas mainly — these blaze, shower rain, illuminate, blow, create and remove the evil activities of living beings. They are glorified as such.
55.59: They destroy the merits of the wicked and the sins of good persons in certain cases.
55.60: They arc seated in an aerial chariot that is divine, that has the speed of the wind and that can go wherever it wills. These move ahead along with the sun throughout the day.
55.61: They shower rain. They blaze, they delight. O Sages, they protect all the living beings and firmament from destruc- tion.
55.62: They take pride and identify themselves with their positions in all the manvantaras of the past, present and future.
55.63: These seven groups live in the sun in groups of fourteen in all the fourteen manvantaras.
55.64: O leading sages, the activities of the intelligent lord of Devas have been recounted, some in brief and some in detail, in accordance with what I have heard and how they had happened.
55.65: These seven groups of twelve deities in each are those who take pride in their positions and identify themselves with them. They reside in the sun for two months in the above order.
55.66: Thus the sun, the harbinger of the day moves ahead quickly in a single-wheeled chariot drawn by seven green imperishable horses.
55.67: He whirls day and night in his chariot which has a single wheel. He traverses in heaven over the seven continents and oceans with the help of seven groups.

56.1: The Moon traverses the stars stationed in its orbit. His chariot has three wheels and the horses are on either side.
56.2: The chariot is fitted with three wheels, each with hund- red spokes. The horses are white in colour and ten in number* They are divine and stout. They are not connected with the yoke. They have the speed of the mind.
56.3: The moon traverses in this chariot along with Devas
56.4: The moon increases in force in the beginning of the bright half and is stationed in the way of the sun. Day by day it gets refilled till the end of that half. The sun develops and nourishes it. It is drunk up bv Devas during the dark half.® It is being drunk in continuity for fifteen days by Devas. The sun refills it part by part by his single ray Susumna: Thus the physical body of the moon is developed and nourished by the vigour of the sun.
56.5: When the fifteenth part remains as the last digit, the groups of Pitrs occupy this in the afternoon. For the dura- tion of two kalas (units of time) they drink up the remaining digit — the nectar of svadha that has oozed out of the rays on the Amavasya day. After drinking the nectar they attain full satiety for the whole of month and then go away. By the time the remaining digit of the moon drunk by the Pitrs gets dissol- ved, a fifteenth part is replenished. The increase and the decrease of the moon in the beginning of each fortnight is on the sixteenth day.®*' The increase in the moon is thus due to the sun.

57.1: The chariot of the son of the Moon (i.e. Budha — Mercury) is fitted with eight horses, tawny-coloured and very Splendid. It has the characteristics of water and fire.
57.2: There are as many rays as there are stars. All of them are bound to the Pole star. While revolving (round it) they make it revolve also.
57.3: The stars and the luminaries, urged by the circular gusts of wind, move like fire brands. Since the wind bears the luminaries, it is called Pravaha.
57.4: Along with the planets and constellations, the sun and stars occupy the firmament in a circle looking upwards and sideways.
57.5: Presided over (i.e. controlled) by Dhruva they circum- ambulate Dhruva. They move on in the firmament to see Lord Dhruva that acts like the pivot.
57.6: Chapters 56-57 describe the movement of the planets Soma, Budha, Mahgala, Brhaspati, Sukra, Sani and Rihu.
57.7: The diameter of the sun is nine thousand Yojanas. Its circular area is three times this.
57.8: The abode of Rahu is full of darkness and is the third (one in size) because it is evolved out of the circular shadow of the earth.
57.9: The diameter, the circumference and the distance in yojanas of Bhargava (Venus) is a sixteenth part of that of the moon.
57.10: Brhaspati (Jupiter) is of three-fourths of the size of Venus. Mars and Saturn are three-fourths of the size of Brhaspati. Budha (Mercury) is three-fourths of their size in extent and circumference. The stars and constellations, that have a body are equal to Budha in extent and circumference. The knower of truth must note that the stars that are in conjun- ction with the moon are ordinarily known as Rksas. The spheres of the comparatively smaller stars extend to five, four, three or two yojanas. Over all these there are still clusters of smaller stars which extend only to two hundred yojanas. There is none smaller than this.
57.11: Over and above these starry spheres are the three planets viz., Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, which travel at a great distance from them. They should be known as slow-moving ones.
57.12: Altogether there are as many crores of stars as there are constellations. They too are stationed in the orbit of con- stellations due to the restraining force of Dhruva,
57.13: The sun that has seven horses has an upper and a lower position by turns. When the sun is in his northern transit and when the moon on the full moon nights, appears quickly because its position is above, but the rays are not very clear, the moon (?) then is in the southern orbit that is lower. The sun covered by the line of the earth on Full moon and New Moon days is seen at the usual time, but it sets quickly. Hence on the New-Moon day the moon is in the northern orbit. It is invariably not seen in the southern path on account of
57.14: In the northern orbits they rise and set without any difference in time on new moon and full moon days. They should then be known as following the groups of luminaries. When the sun is in the southern transit, it moves ahead beneath all other planets.
57.15: Keeping his sphere wider the moon revolves above it (the sun). All the groups of constellations move above the moon.
57.16: Mercury is above all constellations; Venus is above Mercury. Mars is above Venus and Jupiter is above Mars.
57.17: Saturn is above it. Above Saturn is the sphere of seven sages (Great Bear) and Dhruva(Polc Star) is stationed above the seven sages.
57.18: By knowing the region ofVisnu, beyond all these, one is liberated from sin. Two hundred thousand Yojanas above constellations, stars, the planets — Sun and Moon which are united with divine refulgence, move ahead day and night in due order. They come into contact with the constellations everyday. Hence they are sometimes stationed below, some- times above and sometimes in u straight line. They glance at the subjects (below) simultaneously when in conjunction or when separated.

58.1: Tell us now how Brahma Prajapati, who is the soul of all, crowned as overlords, Devas, Daityas and others.
58.2: Lord Brahma crowned the Sun as the overlord of planets. Brahma, Prajapati, crowned Soma (Moon) as the lord of constellations and medicinal herbs.
58.3: (He crowned) Varuna as the lord of the Waters; the leading Yaksa*(Kubera)as the lord of riches; Visnu as the lord of Adityas; and Pavaka (fire) as the lord of Vasus.
58.4: (He crowned) Dak$a as the lord of Prajapatis; Indra as the lord of Maruts; Prahlada, the leading Daitya as the over- lord of Daityas and Danavas.
58.5: (He crowned) Dharma as the overlord of the Pitrs; Nirrti as the overlord of Raksasas; Rudra as the overlord of Paus (Individual Souls) and Nandin, the leader ofGanas,®® as the overlord of Bhutas (goblins).
58.6: (He crowned) Virabhadra as the overlord of heroes; Bhayahkara (the terrible one) as the overlord of Pisacas (ghosts); Camunda who is bowed to by Devas as the sovereign of Mothers.
58.7: (He crowned) lord Nllalohita, lord of the chiefs of Devas, as the overlord of Rudras; the elephant-faced lord Vinayaka, born of Vyoman* as the overlord of obstacles.
58.8: (He crowned ) goddess Uma as the sovereign of women; goddess Sarasvati as the sovereign of speech; Visnu as the overlord of the wielders of Maya and himself®® as the overlord of the worlds.
58.9: (He crowned) Himavat as the overlord of the moun- tains; the Ganges (born of sage Jahnu) as the sovereign of the rivers; and ocean the storehouse of the waters as the lord of all seas.
58.10: vyomajam: son of Siva, i.e. Gaeia.
58.11: sv&tm&nam: his own self, i.e. Brahm&,
58.12: Brahma crowned the Plaksa and Avattha as the lords of trees,* he made Citraratha the lord of Gahdharvas, Vidyadharas and Kinnaras; Vasuki of terrible vigour as the lord of Serpents and Taksaka of terrible vigour as the lord of Safpas (Cobras). He made the leading elephant Airavata of terrible valour the lord of elephants. He made Garuda the lord of birds. He made UccaiiSravas (the horse of Indra) the king of horses.
58.13: He made the lion the lord of animals; the bull the lord of the kine and Sarabha (the fabulous eight-footed beast) the lord of lions; the incomprehensible Guha the lord of all com- manders-in-chief and Lakulisa the lord of Srutis and Smrtis.
58.14: He made Sudharman, Sahkhapala, Ketuman and Hemaroman the overlords of all quarters in order.
58.15: (He crowned) Prthu as the lord of the earth; Mahesvara as the lord of all; the bull-bannered omniscient lord Sankara as the overlord among the four deities.
58.16: By the grace of Siva, the lord crowned these in due order. After crowning them at first the lord of the worlds felt fully satisfied.
58.17: O leading sages, this has been mentioned to you in detail: These persons of special characteristics were all crown- ed by Lord Brahma the source of origin of the universe.

59.1: The four guardian deities, viz. Sudharman, Sahkhapala, Ketu- man, Hemaroman were consecrated in their respective quarters. Gf. Vi?i>u
59.2: caturmurtiu; in four forms, viz. Visva, Prajna, Taijasa, and Turiya.
59.3: O Suta, most excellent among the speakers, kindly tell us in detail the exact nature of the luminaries briefly.
59.4: On hearing their words, Suta of great concentration and purity spoke these weighty words in order to clear their doubts.
59.5: In this matter I shall tell you what has already been stated by highly intelligent persons with tranquil wisdom. I shall recount the movement of the sun and the moon.
59.6: I shall tell you how the sun, the moon and other planets arc the abodes of Devas. Thereafter, I shall mention the three® types of fires and their origin.
59.7: The three types of fire are: the divine fire, the ele- mental fire and the terrestrial fire.
59.8: The fire in the world of mankind is called Parthiva. The fire that blazes in the sun is called iSuci. The fire born of lightning is known as Abja (i.e. originating from the water portion). I shall now mention their characteristics. 7'here are three types of fires with water within, viz., Vaidyuta, Jathara (gastric) and Saura (Solar).
59.9: Hence, imbibing water through his rays the sun blazes ( further). The Abja (waterborn — lightning) fire even when immersed in water is not quenched by it. The fire that is
59.10: mah&pr&jnaih: by the most intelligent men, i.e. by Vyasa and others.
59.11: Threefold fire: (i) celestial, as rep]:esented by the sun, (ii) atmospheric, as smboUzed by the lightning, (iii) terrestrial, which is used for the sacrificial and household purpose. Fire is called Pavaka on earth, Suci in heaven and Vaidyuta in firmament.
59.12: When the sun is setting, the solar lustre becomes a circular mass without heat and enters the fire at night through his rays. Hence the light of fire is seen even from a distance at night. The heat is transmitted to the sun from fire, when the sun rises. Only partially does the terrestrial fire enter the sun. Hence the fire continues to blaze. Thus the fire element in both terrestrial and solar fires contains heat and light. They penetrate mutually and develop each other. In the northern and south- ern hemispheres of the earth, the fire and the sun thus develop each other. The sun rises up from the waters and re-enters them. Therefore, due to this exit (from and into waters) by day and by night, the waters become copper-coloured. Again when the sun sets, the day (i.e. daylight) enters the waters. Hence at night, the waters are seen shining white.
59.13: By means of this activity he enters waters perpetually, during day and night at the time of rising and setting both in the southern and northern hemispheres.
59.14: The sun who blazes, imbibing the waters through his rays has the mixture of earthly and fiery particles within it. It is called divine fire,
59.15: He has a thousand rays emitting snow, rain and heat. Of them four hundred tubular rays have forms of variegated colours. They shower rain. Their collective name is Amrta and the several individual names are Bhajanas, Malyas, Ketanas and Patanas.
59.16: Fire on earth is the symbol of heat and fire in heaven is the symbol of light and both are interdependent. Cf. Matsya. 128.12. STTW
59.17: In the spring the sun is tawny coloured; in the summer he has the lustre of gold. During the rainy season the colour of the sun is white. In the autumn the sun is grey- coloured. In the early winter the sun is copper-coloured and in the late winter he is red in colour.
59.18: The numerous solar rays have their functional division. For instance, four hundred of them funcdon for creating rain (V.24-36), three hundred for heat (V.a8) and three hundred for cold V.26). These rays are distributed over the seasons and bring about the changes of cold, heat and rain.
59.19: The sun infuses strength into the medicinal herbs; he propitiates the Pitrs by means of Svadha rays; he instils nectar into the immortal beings. Thus, he imparts three things to the three groups.

60.1: It is cited' that the sun is fire and the moon is water. The other five planets are known as lords who move about as they please.
60.2: Understand the source of origin of the remaining planets which is clearly being recounted now. It is cited that the planet Mars is Skanda (Karttikeya) the commander-in-chief of the army of Devas.
60.3: People of perfect knowledge say that Mercury is lord Narayana. O excellent brahmins, the great planet Sanaiicara, the slow-moving Saturn is Yama, the lord of the worlds. The preceptors of Devas and Asuras are the great planets Venus and Jupiter with (refulgent) rays. They are mentioned as the sons of Prajapati.®®
60.4: For the celestial fire as identical with the sun, cf. SpT  ted in ST.
60.6: The entire universe including Devas, Asuras and human beings originates from him. He is the lustre of all lumi- naries and the universal refulgence. The refulgence of Rudra, Indra, Upendra, the moon, the leading brahmins, the fire and the heaven-dwellers comes from the sun. He is the soul of all. He is the lord of all worlds. He alone is Mahadeva, PrajS- pati and the lord of the three worlds. He is the originai great deity. Everything originates from him and dissolves in him.
60.7: The existence and non-existence of the worlds origi- nated from the sun formerly. O brahmins, this refulgent sun of great lustre is an incomprehensible planet.
60.8: All these units of time begin from him and end in him again and again, viz., k§anas (moments), muhurtas. a unit of 48 mts.), days, nights, fortnights, months, years, seasons and yugas. Hence without the sun there is no reckoning of time.
60.9: Without Kaia (time) there is no order, no initia- tion, no daily ritual. How can there be the division of the sea- sons? Whence afe these flowers, roots and fruits? Whence is the outcome of plants? How can there be the different kinds of grass and medicinal plants? The dealings of the creatures in heaven and here too will be non-existent without the sun who is the form of Rudra, the scorcher of the universe. He alone is time, fire, Dvadasatman (one having twelve forms) and Praja- pati. O excellent brahmins, he scorches the three worlds includ- ing the mobile and immobile beings. He is the mine of splend- our. He is all in all, the whole set of worlds.
60.10: Adopting the excellent path, he scorches the entire universe from the sides, from above and from below in the course of nights and days.
60.11: If a bright lamp is hung in the middle of the house, it dispels darkness from the sides, the portion above and the portion below, at the same time.
60.12: In the same manner the thousand-rayed sun, the king of planets, the lord of the*universe, illuminates the entire universe by means of his rays.
60.13: Seven rays, that are the source of origin of the planets
60.14: They are Suumna, HarikeSa VKvakarman, ViiSva- vyacas, Sannaddha, Sarvavasu and Svarat*
60.15: Harikea which is in front (in the cast) is glorified as the source of origin of constellations.**®® In the south, the ray Vivakarma develops Budha (Mercury). The ray Vi§vavyacas which is in the west (behind) is the source of origin of Sukra (Venus). The ray Sannaddha is the source of origin of Mars. The ray Sarvavasu is the source of origin of Brhaspati (Jupiter). The ray Svarat nourishes!§anaicara (Saturn). Thus it is due to the power of the sun that the constellations, planets and stars are seen in the heaven. This entire universe is sustained by him. The constellations are called Nakatras. The word is derived from -/ksi with the prohibitive particle 'na' i.c. na klyante (i.c. those which do not perish).

61.1: All these are the abodes which blaze by means of solar rays. The constellations and stars are the abodes to be attained by merits. They arc called Tarakas because they enable people to cross the ocean of worldly existence and also because they arc white.
61.2: The sun is called Aditya because he takes up the divine and terrestrial splendours as well as the nocturnal darkness.
61.3: The principal seven rays, Susumna etc., of the thousand-rayed tun are the source of energy and movement of stars, planets and constella- tions. For instance, the solar ray, called Susumna, causes the movement of the moon.
61.4: dakfiSm rfilim i.e. the moon. The LiAgapura describes vividly the respective fimedons of the seven solar rays.
61.5: The root is used in two meanings to extract juice or to flow. Since the sun extracts refulgence and makes water flow» it is called Savitr.
61.6: The root *cadi' from which the word Gandra is derived means *to delight'. It implies whiteness, chillness, and nectarine nature of the moon (Gandra).
61.7: The divine discs of the sun and the moon are refulgent. They move in the sky. They are white and arc of the nature of fire and water. They arc splendid and they resemble a circular pot.
61.8: The disc of the moon is of the nature of dense water. The disc of the sun is white and is of the nature of dense fire.
61.9: Devas reside in constellations, sun and planets. They live everywhere in these abodes in all the manvantaras.
61.10: Hence the planets arc abodes named after their respec- tive planets. The Sun entered the abode Saura. The Moon entered the abode Saumya.
61.11: Venus entered the abode Saukra. Jupiter, the valorous with sixteen rays entered the abode Bfhad (big). The Mars entered the abode Lohita pertaining to Mars.
61.12: The Saturn entered the abode Sanaicara. The Mer- cury entered the abode Baudha. The evil planet Rahu entered the abode Svarbhwu (named after him).
61.13: The deities of constellations entered all these abodes. These luminaries are the abodes of meritorious souls.
61.14: These abodes have been created by the self born deity. They began to function at the beginning of kalpa and they stay until all the living beings are dissolved.
61.15: In all the manvantaras they alone are the abodes of Devas. These deities who have identified themselves with the abodes occupy these divine abodes again and again.
61.16: They occupy these abodes along with Devas of the past, present and future. In this current manvantara the planets are moving about in aerial chariots.
61.17: Thus the constellations and planets in the sim and the moon as also their abodes and the various deities occupying them have all been mentioned.
61.18: The fiery abode Saura belongs to the thousand-rayed Vivasvan. The abode of the snow-rayed moon is watery and white.
61.19: The abode of Budha (mercury) is watery, dark- coloured and charming. The region of Sukra (Venus) is also watery but white with sixteen rays.
61.20: The abode of Bhauma (Mars) is reddish and it has nine rays. The abode of Bfhaspati (Jupiter) is yellow with sixteen rays and is very large.
61.21: The abode Sani (Saturn) is black with eight rays. The abode of Svarbhanu (Rahu) is gloomy and is a place of great distress to living beings.
61.22: All the stars should be known as the abodes of sages with one ray each. They arc the resorts of men of meritorious renown and are white in colour.
61.23: They are of the nature of dense water (snow). They were created in the beginning of the kalpa. Thanks to the contact with the rays of the sun they have a shining appear- ance.
61.24: The diameter of the sun is nine thousand yojanas. The extent of its circular surface is three times that.
61.25: The extent of the moon is twice that of the sun. Rfihu assumes a form equal to both of them and moves about beneath them.
61.26: Vikeil*: The graha Bhauma (Mahgala) bom of Vikeilis here called agni (fire). Gf. agnir niardba{RV. 8.44.16) wherein Bhauma if called agni. Vikel! it one of the eigdit wivci of the eight-fixrmed (aftamurti) Rudra, others becali, Svavarcalft 'Um&, Sivi, SvShft, Dik, Dikfft and Rohinl.
61.27: Mars and Saturn are a fourth less than Jupiter. In extent and width Mercury is a fourth less than these two.
61.28: The forms of those constellations and stars that are embodied are equal to Mercury in width and circular area.
61.29: The constellations that are in conjunction with the moon are ordinarily known as Rksas. The spheres of the com- paratively smaller stars are five, four, three or two yojanas. Over all these there are clusters of still smaller stars which extend to only half a yojana in width. There is none smaller than this. Over and above these starry spheres are the three planets which move at a great distance from them. They should be known as slow moving ones. The speed of these has already been mentioned in due order.
61.30: All the planets are born of constellations. O excellent sages, the sun, the son of Aditi, the first among the planets, is born of the constellation Viakha. The lustrous son of Dharma, lord Vasu, Soma (moon), the cool-rayed lord of the night, is born of the constellation Krttika. The sixteen-rayed son of Bhrgu, Sukra (Venus) who is the most excellent among the stars and planets after the sun, is born of the constellation Tisya. The planet Brhaspati (Jupiter), the twelve-rayed son of Angiras, the preceptor of the universe, is born of the cons- tellation Purvaphalguni.
61.31: The five-rayed planet Budha (Mercury) the son of the moon is born of the constellation Dhanistha.
61.33: It should be noted that the planets beginning with Bhargava (Venus) are known as star-planets (i.e planets re- sembling stars). Persons who are affected by afflictions from their birthday stars are liberated from that defect by devotion to their respective planets. Ainong all the planets the first one, it is said, is Aditya (Sun).
61.34: Katia has the nimesa as its first unit of tkoe, O excellent ones among the knowers of time. Beginning with the constellation Dhanistha and ending with Sravaa shall be a yuga comprising of five years. The universe whirls like a wheel due to the movement of the sun. Hence the sun is the lord and deity delimiting time. He is the instigator and castigator of tha four types of living beings. Rudra, the lord himself, is the inducer

62.1: O brahmins, when he was asked about this matter by me in former time, Markaiitjieya who is an expert in different sciences said to me as I was desirous of hearing.
62.2: An emperor of great splendour, the best among all those who wield weapons, king Uttanapada, ruled over the earth.
62.3: For Rudra as the life-principle of the sun compare: *bh!yodeti «{lryab***-ted in ST.
62.4: O leading brahmins, Suruci who was proud of her beauty pushed him away. Delighted in her mind she placed her own son on the lap of his father.
62.5: The intelligent boy Dhruva became dejected in his mind because he was unable to occupy the lap of his father. He went to his mother and lamented.
62.6: Overwhelmed by her grief the mother said to her weep- ing son: — "Sumci is the most beloved of her husband. Her son too is likewise.
62.7: You, a son bom of me, a very unfortunate woman, arc also equally unfortunate. Why do you bewail? What for do you weep again and again?

65.12: It was at the time of the horse-sacrifice of Ikvaku that Ila became a Kimpurusa. During the state of Kimpurusa, also Ila is called Sudyumna.
65.13: Then it chanced she was a woman for one month and a man for another. Ila resorted to the house of Budha, the son of Soma. Finding an opportunity she was made to indulge in sexual intercourse by Budha. Pururavas was born as the son of Ila and Budha.
65.14: He was intelligent and the first-born in the line of Soma. He was a devotee of Siva and very valorous. O ascetics, I shall dilate later on the extent of expansion of Iksvaku race.
65.15: O excellent brahmins, Sudyumna had three sons viz.: — Utkala, Gaya and VinataSva.
65.16: The land of Utkala was assigned to Utkala, the western land was given to Vinataiva. Gaya is said to be the excellent city of Gaya.
65.17: In Gaya Devas and the Pitrs are stationed always.
65.18: In view of his feminine nature Sudyumna did not get his share but at the instance of Vasitha, Sudyumna was installed in Pratisthana, as its glorious and righteous king. After attaining kingdom, the highly blessed son of Manu equipped with the characteristics of both man and woman, the king of great renown gave that kingdom to Pururavas.

65.71: Then the king who was well known in the three worlds obtained the hymn of Siva from Tandin. He eulogized the lord, the goal of the devotees, after the approval of Tannin. By the grace of holy lord — Tanejin, the king Tridhanva of great fame attained the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and also the overlordship of Ganas.
65.72: O Brahmins, he who reads this or listens to it or narrates this to the Brahmins, attains the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. In order to obtain release, the following sinners should repeat for a year these names, during the three Sandhyas (morning, midday and dusk) in the temple of Siva or in the region sacred to Siva and they should also worship the lord. They are: — the slayer of a Brahmin, the wine addict, the thief, the defiler of the preceptor's bed, the murderer of a refugee, and the one who commits breach of faith with his friends. So also the slayer of mother, father, warrior and the child in the womb.
